02 — Tokenization

A new BPE tokenizer: 5,000 tokens keep 84% of words whole

How BPE builds tokens: merge the most frequent pair, again and again

Letters-only words that are one token

Vocab sizeWords
1,00064%
2,00074%
5,00084%
10,00089%
20,00094%

Larger vocabulary size

Little difference: more words stay whole, but the vectors get longer and accuracy barely changes.

Larger minimum frequency

No difference: every merged pair already appears hundreds of times, so the tokenizer stays the same.

Training data: 24,904 reviews (5.8M words) are enough for a tokenizer made for movie reviews, not a general-purpose one

2 / 7

We did not reuse the tutorial tokenizer: we trained a new BPE tokenizer with the tutorial’s train_tokenizer helper, on the 24,904 IMDB training reviews (about 5.8 million words, the same kind of text as the task), so no larger corpus was needed. The figure is a toy example of how BPE training works, on five movie words used once each (cast, part, scary, star, stars): start from single letters, count every pair of neighbouring tokens, and merge the most frequent pair into a new token. a + r appears in 4 words, so it is merged first; then s + t (3 words), then st + ar, which makes the whole word star (2 words). Training repeats this until the vocabulary has 5,000 tokens (vocab size), and only merges pairs seen at least 2 times (min frequency). We tried vocab sizes 1,000 to 10,000 and min frequency 2 to 5, with only minor changes from 5,000 up. Raw text, no lowercasing; the Metaspace pre-tokenizer splits on spaces first. How many words are one token, counting letters-only words in the training reviews (BPE merges are a prefix of a 20,000-vocab run on the same data): 64% at vocab 1,000, 84% at 5,000, 89% at 10,000, 94% at 20,000. The first merges cover the common words; later merges build rarer words, so gains slow down after 5,000. Min frequency had no effect: any value from 1 to 282 gives exactly the same 4,821 merges (tested 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200), because the last pair merged before reaching 5,000 tokens still occurs 282 times; only above 282 does it cut merges (300: 4,610; 500: 3,209; 1,000: 1,918). Be ready for: the tokenizer saw all training texts, including the validation folds (without labels).

03 — Representation spaces

Three spaces, each giving 5,000 features per review

Training review #11925 (negative)

“This is without a doubt the worst movie I have ever seen. It is not funny. It is not interesting and should not have been made.”

Why log counts: saying “great” 10 times is more positive than once, but not 10 times more, and frequent words like “the” stay small

3 / 7

All three give one number per vocabulary token, so 5,000 numbers per review. Token indicator (tutorial): 1 if the token appears, else 0. Bag of words (tutorial): how many times it appears. Log counts (our addition): log(1 + count). It keeps the information that a token appears several times, but squashes large counts so very frequent tokens do not dominate. Saying “great” five times is more positive than once, but not five times more.

04 — Architectures

One linear model, two multilayer perceptrons

Tried different hyperparameters: minor changes, final setup: learning rate 1e-4, decay 1e-4, dropout 0.1, one hidden layer, 16 units

05 — Evaluation

A hidden layer adds 1–2% accuracy; its size barely matters

Validation accuracy, 15 folds

Bayesian comparison, ROPE 0.5% · decided only if P ≥ 0.95

Strength and limit: 5-fold cross-validation × 3 seeds gives reliable comparisons, but validation data is not truly unseen

5 / 7

Best pick: MLP with 16 units on log counts, 88.17%. Both MLPs are about 1 to 2.6 points above logistic regression, more than the ROPE. Shrinking the MLP from 128 to 16 units costs nothing (over 99% practically the same), so we prefer the smaller, cheaper model. Log counts is the top representation everywhere, but it only clearly wins for logistic regression (86% probability); for the MLPs all three representations are within the ROPE of each other.

Verdict at the end

“the weakest film in the original Star Wars trilogy … a winner”

#13279 · label positive · model 1% pos.

Praise, then “but”

“He is a great comedian but this is not his best movie”

#10931 · label negative · model 94% pos.

Where errors come from: word counts miss context like irony and mixed opinions, and some labels contradict the text

6 / 7

On the 24,678 test reviews, all 15 models predict every review: 6.8% are wrong in all 15, 80.8% right in all 15, 12.4% split (mean test error 12.1%). More examples: #19144 (positive) praises a so-bad-it’s-good film with words like ghastly, dismal, dreadful; #13279 (positive) starts with “the weakest film” and only reaches its verdict at the end; #10931 (negative) praises the comedian but not the film. Error analysis (16-unit MLP, log counts, validation folds): 11.8% of reviews are misclassified; 9.1% are wrong in all three seeds, so errors come mostly from the reviews themselves. Irony (review #24092, positive: “stupid … in a good way”) and genre-fan reviews of bad films use negative words for a positive verdict; mixed reviews (#1391, negative) praise one aspect and reject the film, and counting words cannot tell which sentence carries the verdict; some labels look wrong (#3027 reads clearly positive but is labelled negative). Reviews with but/however have 12.3% error vs 9.6% without; with “not good/not bad” 16.7%. All numbers are on the validation folds: each of the 15 models (5 folds times 3 seeds) is scored on its own held-out fold of about 5,000 training reviews, then averaged. Accuracy matches the saved cross-validation results exactly; F1 (macro), precision and recall (positive class) were computed afterwards from the same saved models. F1 equals accuracy because the classes are balanced. The 16-unit MLP ties the 128-unit MLP on accuracy and F1, has slightly higher recall (0.888 vs 0.886) and slightly lower precision (0.878 vs 0.879). Model size: about 80,000 parameters against 640,000. Bayesian comparison (validation, ROPE 0.5 points): the 16-unit MLP beats logistic regression with probability 1.00 and is practically the same as the 128-unit MLP with probability 0.999.
